key_insight: This paper shows that pretraining data poisoning is feasible even in realistic, large-scale, heterogeneous web corpora—not just in controlled sources like Wikipedia. It also highlights that data curation pipelines can interact with poisoned data in ways that make attacks harder to notice and mitigate.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between prior poisoning research and real-world pretraining pipelines, where data comes from diverse sources and is filtered/curated before training. It asks whether attackers can still inject harmful behaviors into LMs under these more realistic conditions.
method: Demonstrates poisoning attacks on pretraining data beyond narrow, well-structured datasets.
Studies how poisoned samples behave within large, heterogeneous corpus collection and curation pipelines.
Evaluates the feasibility of introducing harmful model behaviors even when data undergoes preprocessing and filtering.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this raises the bar for securing training data and auditing pretraining pipelines. It suggests that defenses must consider not only source trustworthiness but also how curation and filtering may fail to remove targeted poison.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing web-scale data collection -> curation/filtering -> pretraining -> poisoned model behavior
Side-by-side comparison of clean vs poisoned corpus examples
Flowchart illustrating how a poison sample survives curation steps
Risk icon set highlighting detection difficulty, scale, and downstream model harm
paper_title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
paper_authors: Victoria Graf, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Noah A. Smith, David Kohlbrenner, Kyle Lo
